tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

Done. Here’s what I set up for the canary:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80
  - Security configuration matches the stable deployment (no additional securityContext set)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine
  - Selector broadened to app=recommendation-engine (was app + version=v2.0)
  - Ports unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (kept consistent with the existing service)

Result/verification:
- Pods now include:
  - 2x engine-v2-0 (v2.0, stable)
  - 2x engine-v2-1 (v2.1, canary)
- With 2 pods each and a shared Service selector, traffic will be balanced approximately 50/50 across stable and canary.

Adjusting the split:
- Increase/decrease replicas on either Deployment to change the weight (e.g., scale canary to 1 for ~33%, or to 3 for ~60%).
- To roll back to 100% stable quickly, either scale engine-v2-1 to 0 or set the Service selector back to include version=v2.0 only.

If you want me to pin the Service to a specific targetPort (e.g., switch to 80) or add explicit securityContext settings (runAsUser, runAsNonRoot), say the word and I’ll update both deployments consistently.

Diagnosis
- The app Deployment was overriding the container command with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing the pod to exit immediately and enter CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the nginx-unprivileged image uses its default, valid entrypoint.
- Recreated the Deployment cleanly and exposed containerPort 8080 (the unprivileged nginx default).
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

Current status
- Deployment app is healthy.
- Pod app-c88f5d4bc-mlbwp: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts (namespace crashloop-test).

Optional next steps
- If you intended to run a custom command, let me know the correct one and I’ll update the Deployment safely.
- Want me to add a Service to expose it on port 8080, set resource requests/limits, or add health probes?

results.taskOutput:

Done. The pod is now running.

What happened
- The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC homepage-pvc was Pending. Events showed: storageclass “sc” not found.
- Your PVC requested storageClassName: sc, but no such StorageClass existed.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to bind the PVC.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to PV pvc-9c3535b2-4088-4fe9-9b17-4df73208d04c.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, IP 10.244.0.26, container nginx started.

Optional follow-ups
- If you’d prefer not to keep the new “sc” class, we can instead update the PVC to use the existing default StorageClass “standard” and remove “sc.”

Done. The pod is now running.

What happened
- The pod couldn’t schedule because its PVC homepage-pvc was Pending. Events showed: storageclass “sc” not found.
- Your PVC requested storageClassName: sc, but no such StorageClass existed.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc using the cluster’s hostpath provisioner (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath). This allowed dynamic provisioning to bind the PVC.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to PV pvc-9c3535b2-4088-4fe9-9b17-4df73208d04c.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster, IP 10.244.0.26, container nginx started.

Optional follow-ups
- If you’d prefer not to keep the new “sc” class, we can instead update the PVC to use the existing default StorageClass “standard” and remove “sc.”

results.taskOutput:
I’ve fixed it.

What was wrong
- The deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were checking http://:80 on paths /is_ready and /get_status (which don’t exist)
  - The Service targetPort was 80
- Result: readiness/liveness failed and the app wasn’t reachable.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 as-is; it’s just metadata)
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80)

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7455c67864-7j9gk is 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints now point to the pod on 8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/  (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you actually need custom health endpoints or to listen on port 80, I can:
- Configure NGINX to expose those paths, or
- Switch to a root-capable image/set capabilities to bind to 80
- Add an Ingress/Route for external access

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I’ve fixed it.

What was wrong
- The deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were checking http://:80 on paths /is_ready and /get_status (which don’t exist)
  - The Service targetPort was 80
- Result: readiness/liveness failed and the app wasn’t reachable.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 as-is; it’s just metadata)
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80)

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7455c67864-7j9gk is 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints now point to the pod on 8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/  (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you actually need custom health endpoints or to listen on port 80, I can:
- Configure NGINX to expose those paths, or
- Switch to a root-capable image/set capabilities to bind to 80
- Add an Ingress/Route for external access

outputSteps.content:
I’ve fixed it.

What was wrong
- The deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were checking http://:80 on paths /is_ready and /get_status (which don’t exist)
  - The Service targetPort was 80
- Result: readiness/liveness failed and the app wasn’t reachable.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Set readinessProbe and livenessProbe to GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 as-is; it’s just metadata)
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80)

Current status
- Pod is healthy: webapp-7455c67864-7j9gk is 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints now point to the pod on 8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
- curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/  (should return the NGINX welcome page)

If you actually need custom health endpoints or to listen on port 80, I can:
- Configure NGINX to expose those paths, or
- Switch to a root-capable image/set capabilities to bind to 80
- Add an Ingress/Route for external access

Want me to set up an Ingress or scale the deployment?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant any permission on pods. Even though the RoleBinding correctly bound that Role to the pod-reader service account, the service account had no rights to list pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role to include permissions on core API pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing deployments.apps list rule.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader (unchanged)
- RoleBinding: pod-reader-binding binding that SA to Role/pod-reader-role (unchanged)
- Role: pod-reader-role now grants get/list/watch on pods in simple-rbac-setup

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expected: lists pods in that namespace

Note
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant any permission on pods. Even though the RoleBinding correctly bound that Role to the pod-reader service account, the service account had no rights to list pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role to include permissions on core API pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing deployments.apps list rule.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader (unchanged)
- RoleBinding: pod-reader-binding binding that SA to Role/pod-reader-role (unchanged)
- Role: pod-reader-role now grants get/list/watch on pods in simple-rbac-setup

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expected: lists pods in that namespace

Note
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only allowed listing deployments (apps group) and did not grant any permission on pods. Even though the RoleBinding correctly bound that Role to the pod-reader service account, the service account had no rights to list pods.

What I changed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role to include permissions on core API pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - Kept the existing deployments.apps list rule.

Current state
- ServiceAccount: simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader (unchanged)
- RoleBinding: pod-reader-binding binding that SA to Role/pod-reader-role (unchanged)
- Role: pod-reader-role now grants get/list/watch on pods in simple-rbac-setup

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - Expected: yes
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expected: lists pods in that namespace

Note
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. If you need to list pods cluster-wide, use a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic could not reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state
- Pod: web/nginx-6d94b64d45-s9j29 is Running.
- Service: web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.103.195.113:80) now has Endpoints pointing at the Pod on port 8080.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.103.195.113

If you need external access
- There is no Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort defined. Tell me your preference and I can:
  - Create an Ingress to expose it via your ingress controller (recommended)
  - Switch Service type to NodePort
  - Or set up a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)

Optional quick test from your machine
- kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
- Then open http://localhost:8080

Would you like me to expose it externally via an Ingress or NodePort?

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic could not reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state
- Pod: web/nginx-6d94b64d45-s9j29 is Running.
- Service: web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.103.195.113:80) now has Endpoints pointing at the Pod on port 8080.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.103.195.113

If you need external access
- There is no Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort defined. Tell me your preference and I can:
  - Create an Ingress to expose it via your ingress controller (recommended)
  - Switch Service type to NodePort
  - Or set up a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)

Optional quick test from your machine
- kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
- Then open http://localhost:8080

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic could not reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080

Current state
- Pod: web/nginx-6d94b64d45-s9j29 is Running.
- Service: web/nginx (ClusterIP 10.103.195.113:80) now has Endpoints pointing at the Pod on port 8080.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From any Pod in the cluster:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local
  - or curl http://10.103.195.113

If you need external access
- There is no Ingress/LoadBalancer/NodePort defined. Tell me your preference and I can:
  - Create an Ingress to expose it via your ingress controller (recommended)
  - Switch Service type to NodePort
  - Or set up a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)

Optional quick test from your machine
- kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
- Then open http://localhost:8080

Would you like me to expose it externally via an Ingress or NodePort?

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Your web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node.
- Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no nodes with that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
- Because no pods were running, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (kept replicas=2 and the same image).
- Result: both replicas are now Running and the Service has healthy endpoints on port 80.

Current state
- Pods:
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-6758v — 1/1 Running
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-s5zg8 — 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include:
  - 10.244.0.31:80
  - 10.244.0.32:80

Why this caused “connection refused”
- With zero endpoints behind a ClusterIP Service, kube-proxy has nothing to forward to; clients typically receive a TCP RST/connection refused.

Optional follow-ups
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you really need GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the appropriate node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment to use the correct label(s)/tolerations for your environment.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe so traffic only routes when the app is ready.
- Add resource requests/limits for better scheduling and stability.

Tell me if you want me to:
- Reintroduce a correct nodeSelector/affinity and label nodes accordingly.
- Add readiness/liveness probes and resource limits.
- Run an in-cluster curl check to verify HTTP 200 from the Service.

namespace/webshop-frontend created

deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created

deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Your web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node.
- Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no nodes with that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
- Because no pods were running, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (kept replicas=2 and the same image).
- Result: both replicas are now Running and the Service has healthy endpoints on port 80.

- Pods:

- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include:
  - 10.244.0.31:80
  - 10.244.0.32:80

Why this caused “connection refused”
- With zero endpoints behind a ClusterIP Service, kube-proxy has nothing to forward to; clients typically receive a TCP RST/connection refused.

Optional follow-ups
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you really need GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the appropriate node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment to use the correct label(s)/tolerations for your environment.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe so traffic only routes when the app is ready.
- Add resource requests/limits for better scheduling and stability.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Your web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any node.
- Deployment spec had nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster has no nodes with that label. Events showed FailedScheduling: “didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.”
- Because no pods were running, the Service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed to fix it
- Removed the invalid nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (kept replicas=2 and the same image).
- Result: both replicas are now Running and the Service has healthy endpoints on port 80.

Current state
- Pods:
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-6758v — 1/1 Running
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-s5zg8 — 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include:
  - 10.244.0.31:80
  - 10.244.0.32:80

Why this caused “connection refused”
- With zero endpoints behind a ClusterIP Service, kube-proxy has nothing to forward to; clients typically receive a TCP RST/connection refused.

Optional follow-ups
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you really need GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the appropriate node(s) with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment to use the correct label(s)/tolerations for your environment.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe so traffic only routes when the app is ready.
- Add resource requests/limits for better scheduling and stability.

Tell me if you want me to:
- Reintroduce a correct nodeSelector/affinity and label nodes accordingly.
- Add readiness/liveness probes and resource limits.
- Run an in-cluster curl check to verify HTTP 200 from the Service.

What I changed:
- Updated PersistentVolumeClaim resize-pv/storage-pvc request from 1Gi to 3Gi.

- StorageClass csi-hostpath-sc allows expansion.

- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny in every created namespace (Ingress and Egress)
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress+Egress) so workloads in the same namespace can communicate
- DNS and system services allowed for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Egress to kube-system namespace (general system services)
- Developer namespace scoping:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
    - Egress allowed only to same namespace and to dev-shared
    - No ingress from other namespaces
  - In dev-shared:
    - Ingress explicitly allowed only from developer namespaces (namespaceSelector matching env=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie])
    - No egress to developer namespaces (only same-namespace and kube-system/DNS)
- Staging and prod isolation:
  - Default deny for both Ingress and Egress
  - Only same-namespace traffic allowed
  - Only DNS/kube-system egress allowed
  - No dev namespaces can reach staging/prod due to egress restrictions in dev namespaces and deny in staging/prod

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*; dev-shared; staging; prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified

Verification tips (run as cluster-admin)
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding devs-view -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding alice-admin -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy -o name
- kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy -o name
- Test access by impersonation (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice

Notes
- The RoleBinding subjects for Users (alice, bob, charlie) assume those identities are provided by your authn method (client certs/OIDC/etc.). If you use groups, we can switch to group subjects.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, OVN-K8s).
- If you want default container requests/limits and to prevent oversized single Pods, consider adding LimitRanges per namespace (optional).

If you want, I can also generate a single consolidated YAML manifest or add LimitRanges and PodSecurity admission settings for stronger workload safeguards.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested configuration has been created and enforced in the cluster. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for targeting by policies:
  - dev-alice: {env: dev, tenant: alice}
  - dev-bob: {env: dev, tenant: bob}
  - dev-charlie: {env: dev, tenant: charlie}
  - dev-shared: {role: dev-shared}
  - staging: {env: staging}
  - prod: {env: prod}

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts per developer:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings bind alice and dev-alice/alice-sa to ClusterRole admin in dev-alice
  - Same pattern for bob in dev-bob and charlie in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-view in dev-shared binds Users alice, bob, charlie and SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod restricted:
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; access defaults to deny. Cluster admins (system:masters/cluster-admin) retain access via existing cluster-wide bindings

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2, limits.memory: 4Gi, requests.cpu: 2, requests.memory: 4Gi, pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny in every created namespace (Ingress and Egress)
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress+Egress) so workloads in the same namespace can communicate
- DNS and system services allowed for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Egress to kube-system namespace (general system services)
- Developer namespace scoping:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
    - Egress allowed only to same namespace and to dev-shared
    - No ingress from other namespaces
  - In dev-shared:
    - Ingress explicitly allowed only from developer namespaces (namespaceSelector matching env=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie])
    - No egress to developer namespaces (only same-namespace and kube-system/DNS)
- Staging and prod isolation:
  - Default deny for both Ingress and Egress
  - Only same-namespace traffic allowed
  - Only DNS/kube-system egress allowed
  - No dev namespaces can reach staging/prod due to egress restrictions in dev namespaces and deny in staging/prod

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*; dev-shared; staging; prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified

Verification tips (run as cluster-admin)
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding devs-view -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding alice-admin -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy -o name
- kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy -o name
- Test access by impersonation (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice

Notes
- The RoleBinding subjects for Users (alice, bob, charlie) assume those identities are provided by your authn method (client certs/OIDC/etc.). If you use groups, we can switch to group subjects.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, OVN-K8s).
- If you want default container requests/limits and to prevent oversized single Pods, consider adding LimitRanges per namespace (optional).

If you want, I can also generate a single consolidated YAML manifest or add LimitRanges and PodSecurity admission settings for stronger workload safeguards.

All requested configuration has been created and enforced in the cluster. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for targeting by policies:
  - dev-alice: {env: dev, tenant: alice}
  - dev-bob: {env: dev, tenant: bob}
  - dev-charlie: {env: dev, tenant: charlie}
  - dev-shared: {role: dev-shared}
  - staging: {env: staging}
  - prod: {env: prod}

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts per developer:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings bind alice and dev-alice/alice-sa to ClusterRole admin in dev-alice
  - Same pattern for bob in dev-bob and charlie in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-view in dev-shared binds Users alice, bob, charlie and SAs dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod restricted:
  - No developer bindings in staging/prod; access defaults to deny. Cluster admins (system:masters/cluster-admin) retain access via existing cluster-wide bindings

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2, limits.memory: 4Gi, requests.cpu: 2, requests.memory: 4Gi, pods: 10, services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi, requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi, pods: 20, services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi, requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi, pods: 50, services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny in every created namespace (Ingress and Egress)
- Same-namespace allow (Ingress+Egress) so workloads in the same namespace can communicate
- DNS and system services allowed for all namespaces:
  - Egress to kube-dns/coredns on TCP/UDP 53
  - Egress to kube-system namespace (general system services)
- Developer namespace scoping:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
    - Egress allowed only to same namespace and to dev-shared
    - No ingress from other namespaces
  - In dev-shared:
    - Ingress explicitly allowed only from developer namespaces (namespaceSelector matching env=dev and tenant in [alice, bob, charlie])
    - No egress to developer namespaces (only same-namespace and kube-system/DNS)
- Staging and prod isolation:
  - Default deny for both Ingress and Egress
  - Only same-namespace traffic allowed
  - Only DNS/kube-system egress allowed
  - No dev namespaces can reach staging/prod due to egress restrictions in dev namespaces and deny in staging/prod

5) Default Deny
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*; dev-shared; staging; prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified

Verification tips (run as cluster-admin)
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebinding devs-view -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebinding alice-admin -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota -o yaml
- kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy -o name
- kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy -o name
- Test access by impersonation (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice

Notes
- The RoleBinding subjects for Users (alice, bob, charlie) assume those identities are provided by your authn method (client certs/OIDC/etc.). If you use groups, we can switch to group subjects.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, OVN-K8s).
- If you want default container requests/limits and to prevent oversized single Pods, consider adding LimitRanges per namespace (optional).

If you want, I can also generate a single consolidated YAML manifest or add LimitRanges and PodSecurity admission settings for stronger workload safeguards.

- The PipelineRun fails during reconciliation because the referenced Task is missing.

  - The Pipeline “broken-pipeline” in tekton-eval has a single taskRef: name: missing-task.
  - No Task named missing-task exists in any namespace, and no ClusterTask CRD is installed.
  - No TaskRun pod was ever started; controller failed before scheduling.

Pipeline-as-Code (PaC) and TektonConfig context
- Pipelines-as-Code CRDs (pipelinesascode.tekton.dev) are not installed: no matches for kind "Repository".
  - If you expected PaC to pull Tasks from your repo automatically, it isn’t active in this cluster/namespace.
- Tekton Operator’s TektonConfig CRD is not installed (operator.tekton.dev): no matches for kind "TektonConfig".
  - Feature flags visible in the PipelineRun status (enableAPIFields: beta, etc.) indicate Tekton Pipelines is running, but nothing suggests remote resolvers are being used for taskRef.
- Net effect: taskRef without a resolver requires a namespaced Task object to exist; since it doesn’t, the run cannot start.

Recommended next action
Pick one of the following, depending on intent:

1) If you intended a local Task
- Create a Task named missing-task in namespace tekton-eval (or rename the pipeline’s taskRef to an existing Task).
- Example skeleton:
  - apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
  - kind: Task
  - metadata: name: missing-task; namespace: tekton-eval
  - spec:
    - steps:
      - name: run
        image: bash:5
        script: |
          echo "hello from missing-task"
- Then restart the PipelineRun (or start a new one).

2) If you intended to use a Tekton Hub/Catalog or Git/OCI-resolved Task
- Update the pipeline to use a resolver-based taskRef (and ensure the relevant resolvers are installed/enabled), for example:
  - taskRef:
      resolver: hub
      params:
      - name: name
        value: git-clone
      - name: version
        value: "0.9"
  - Or use git/oci bundle resolvers with appropriate params (url/revision/path or bundle image).
- Then restart the PipelineRun.

3) If you expected Pipelines-as-Code to supply tasks from your repo
- Install/configure Pipelines-as-Code and create a Repository in tekton-eval (or in the controller’s watched namespaces), push your .tekton/ pipeline and tasks, and trigger a new run via a PR or push.

- After fixing the Task reference, restart the run:
  - tkn pipelinerun delete failed-run -n tekton-eval (optional) and re-trigger, or
  - tkn pipelinerun start broken-pipeline -n tekton-eval (with required params/workspaces), or

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The PipelineRun fails during reconciliation because the referenced Task is missing.
- Evidence:
  - PipelineRun status: CouldntGetTask — “Couldn't retrieve Task 'missing-task': tasks.tekton.dev 'missing-task' not found”.
  - The Pipeline “broken-pipeline” in tekton-eval has a single taskRef: name: missing-task.
  - No Task named missing-task exists in any namespace, and no ClusterTask CRD is installed.
  - No TaskRun pod was ever started; controller failed before scheduling.

Pipeline-as-Code (PaC) and TektonConfig context
- Pipelines-as-Code CRDs (pipelinesascode.tekton.dev) are not installed: no matches for kind "Repository".
  - If you expected PaC to pull Tasks from your repo automatically, it isn’t active in this cluster/namespace.
- Tekton Operator’s TektonConfig CRD is not installed (operator.tekton.dev): no matches for kind "TektonConfig".
  - Feature flags visible in the PipelineRun status (enableAPIFields: beta, etc.) indicate Tekton Pipelines is running, but nothing suggests remote resolvers are being used for taskRef.
- Net effect: taskRef without a resolver requires a namespaced Task object to exist; since it doesn’t, the run cannot start.

Recommended next action
Pick one of the following, depending on intent:

1) If you intended a local Task
- Create a Task named missing-task in namespace tekton-eval (or rename the pipeline’s taskRef to an existing Task).
- Example skeleton:
  - apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
  - kind: Task
  - metadata: name: missing-task; namespace: tekton-eval
  - spec:
    - steps:
      - name: run
        image: bash:5
        script: |
          echo "hello from missing-task"
- Then restart the PipelineRun (or start a new one).

2) If you intended to use a Tekton Hub/Catalog or Git/OCI-resolved Task
- Update the pipeline to use a resolver-based taskRef (and ensure the relevant resolvers are installed/enabled), for example:
  - taskRef:
      resolver: hub
      params:
      - name: name
        value: git-clone
      - name: version
        value: "0.9"
  - Or use git/oci bundle resolvers with appropriate params (url/revision/path or bundle image).
- Then restart the PipelineRun.

3) If you expected Pipelines-as-Code to supply tasks from your repo
- Install/configure Pipelines-as-Code and create a Repository in tekton-eval (or in the controller’s watched namespaces), push your .tekton/ pipeline and tasks, and trigger a new run via a PR or push.

Operational follow-up
- After fixing the Task reference, restart the run:
  - tkn pipelinerun delete failed-run -n tekton-eval (optional) and re-trigger, or
  - tkn pipelinerun start broken-pipeline -n tekton-eval (with required params/workspaces), or
  - Restart the existing run if you prefer to keep history consistent.

Given the current state, the fastest fix is to create the missing Task (or correct the taskRef name) in tekton-eval and rerun.
